newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Singapore motorists bleat at new curbs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Singapore motorists bleat at new curbs.

text.p: Wealthy Singapore's latest idea to prevent the tiny island from being submerged by cars has not won much of a welcome from motorists.
The pay-as-you-use Road Pricing Scheme (RPS) was introduced to ease rush-hour congestion on the busiest stretches of roads as the number of cars goes on rising.

Singapore's car policies have been largely successful in the past. The city's worst traffic jams pale into insignificance in comparison to the gridlocks of other major Asian cities like Bangkok and Jakarta.
Seven years ago the government introduced its most significant measure, the Certificate of Entitlement (COE), effectively a licence to own a car.
COEs, auctioned monthly and valid for 10 years, are sold at huge cost in limited numbers. On expiry they can be renewed at the average cost over the previous 12 months.

For a car with an engine capacity below 1000 cc, a COE currently costs S$41,008 (US$28,165). For a mid-sized car of up to 1,600 cc it costs S$62,208 and up to 2,000 cc, the price is S$73,351. For cars above 2000 cc, a COE is S$73,500.

Then there is the cost of the car itself. Add that to the COE and the total price of a typical small car is S$81,888. A Mercedes Benz can cost S$264,500. Singapore's annual road tax is also expensive -- about S$668 for a small car and S$2,869 for a big one. HIGH DEMAND
The government earned S$2 billion in 1996 from auctioning COEs and their prices are expected to go on rising over the long term in response to high demand.
That S$2 billion was used to finance public transport infrastructure, said Zainul Abidin, a Land Transport Authority spokesman.
Singapore encourages people to use an extensive public transport system including bus and Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) rail networkS, or to take taxis.
But still the demand for cars is unabated despite additional costs of S$60 a month for a pass for motorists who want to drive into the city centre during business hours.
Three of the island's main expressways, the East Coast Parkway (ECP), the 41-km long Pan-Island expressway (PIE) and the Central Expressway (CTE) are becoming increasingly congested.

The Road Pricing System was introduced in 1995 on the ECP. Motorists had to buy a sticker at $2 a day or $40 a month to use the highway during morning and evening rush hours. The scheme was extended to the PIE and CTE in May.
Analysts say that as a result of all these measures, average speeds in Singapore's inner city are the fastest in Asia.
Nevertheless, the scheme has its critics.
The expressways are less busy at rush hours, but people are simply switching to feeder roads which have become more congested, drivers complain.
"Singapore's Road Pricing Scheme is a means of raising tax revenue and an ineffective method of traffic management," said businessman Peter Ho.
Another businessman, who declined to be identified, shared that view.
"If congestion is there, that means the expressways were not designed properly to manage it," he said. "RPS is not the technical solution."
But Automobile Association of Singapore (AAS) president Gerard Ee told Reuters there was no alternative to RPS, which he defended as "an effective usage-based mechanism". UNAVOIDABLE CONGESTION
"Traffic on the PIE reduced by about 25 percent and average travel speeds improved to above 65 kilometres per hour," Abidin told Reuters in a written response to questions.
The congestion on the side roads was expected, and was unavoidable as long as people refused to pay to drive on the expressways, he said.
"Drivers have the option of taking the express bus services availiable from May, staggering time or using public transport," Abidin said.
Ho predicted that congestion would soon reappear on the expressways. "I'd only give it six months," he said.

"How long will people, especially businessmen, tolerate jams off the expressways if they only have to pay $2 to use them?," Ho asked. The next logical step would be to see RPS charges raised to even more prohibitive levels.
Government officials are more optimistic. They said they hoped the RPS would encourage drivers to use public transport.
But many drivers say they are reluctant to give up their cars.
"Where will it end?," Ho said. "God knows how many labels you'll need on your windshield to drive in Singapore soon."
